datasetName: MindMate AI Chatbot Supportive Guidance Dataset
intendedUse: Grounding/retrieval dataset for a university mental-health supportive chatbot. Not a diagnostic tool.
safetyNotice: This chatbot should not diagnose, treat, or replace licensed mental-health professionals. High-risk messages should trigger human handoff or emergency guidance.

severityDefinitions.low: Everyday stress or emotional concern; self-help guidance may be appropriate.
severityDefinitions.moderate: Ongoing or distressing concern; encourage trusted support or counselor contact.
severityDefinitions.high: Safety, abuse, severe impairment, or urgent concern; human handoff recommended.
severityDefinitions.imminent: Immediate self-harm/violence/emergency risk; emergency response required.

entries.response: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of academic responsibilities right now, and that can be exhausting. Many students experience stress when balancing assignments, projects, deadlines, and personal responsibilities. Remember that feeling stressed does not mean you are incapable-it often means you are trying your best to meet important goals. Take things one step at a time, celebrate even small accomplishments, and give yourself credit for the effort you have already made. Progress is built through consistent effort, not perfection.

Source: WHO (2022) https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mental-health-strengthening-our-response

entries.response: Your safety comes first. If someone may hurt you or you are in immediate danger, move to a safer place if possible and contact emergency services or a trusted authority. You deserve protection and support without blame.
entries.evidenceSummary: WHO identifies violence as a serious public-health issue with physical and mental-health consequences. Trauma-informed guidance recommends safety-oriented, non-blaming support.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Being bullied or humiliated can deeply affect your well-being. This is not your fault. Save evidence when it is safe, avoid responding to harmful messages, and reach out to a trusted teacher, adviser, supervisor, or support office.
entries.evidenceSummary: StopBullying.gov defines bullying as unwanted aggressive behavior involving a power imbalance and repetition or likelihood of repetition, including cyberbullying contexts.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Using alcohol or substances to cope can feel like temporary relief, but it can make stress and safety risks worse over time. Consider speaking with a counselor, healthcare provider, or trusted support service for safer coping options.
entries.evidenceSummary: WHO discusses health and social harms related to alcohol, and SAMHSA provides referral resources for mental-health and substance-use concerns.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Managing time is easier when tasks are visible and small. Try listing your tasks, choosing the most urgent one, and working in short focused blocks with breaks. Progress matters more than doing everything perfectly at once.
entries.evidenceSummary: APA and WHO stress-management resources support realistic planning, manageable goals, rest, and coping strategies for daily demands.

sources.title: Doing what matters in times of stress

entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Starting can be the hardest part. Try making the task smaller: open the file, write one sentence, or study for five minutes. A small start can reduce pressure and build momentum.
entries.evidenceSummary: Stress-management and self-care guidance from WHO and APA supports breaking demands into manageable actions and using practical coping strategies.

sources.title: Doing what matters in times of stress

entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Feeling like you do not belong can happen even when you are working hard and learning. Your doubts are not proof that you are failing. Try noticing evidence of effort, progress, and feedback instead of focusing only on mistakes.
entries.evidenceSummary: APA resources on self-esteem and self-efficacy discuss confidence, learning, and personal agency as skills that develop through experience.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Losing someone or something important can affect your emotions, focus, sleep, and energy. There is no single correct way to grieve. Allow yourself support from trusted people, and consider professional help if grief feels unbearable or unsafe.
entries.evidenceSummary: NIMH caring-for-your-mental-health guidance encourages seeking support when emotional distress affects daily life; trauma-informed guidance supports compassionate, non-judgmental care.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Wanting to do well can be healthy, but needing everything to be perfect can become exhausting. Try aiming for clear progress, realistic standards, and learning from mistakes instead of treating mistakes as failure.
entries.evidenceSummary: APA stress and resilience resources discuss realistic expectations, coping, and learning from challenges as part of well-being.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Feeling nervous before speaking in front of others is common. Prepare your key points, practice in small steps, and focus on communicating one idea at a time. Confidence usually grows through repeated experience.
entries.evidenceSummary: APA anxiety resources describe anxiety as a common response and emphasize coping strategies and preparation for managing excessive worry.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.

entries.response: Adjusting to a new environment takes time. It is normal to feel unsure while learning routines, expectations, and relationships. Build small habits, ask questions, and give yourself time to adapt.
entries.evidenceSummary: WHO and APA resilience resources describe adaptation, social support, and coping skills as important parts of well-being during change.
entries.clinicalDisclaimer: This is supportive guidance only and does not replace assessment by a licensed mental-health professional.
